records.sourceFile: The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury - A Scoping Review.pdf

paper.citation: Meredith S, Farley JB, Hunt J, Dent E. The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:148.
paper.abstract: Scoping review of seven studies on psychosocial factors and return to physical activity and sport in female football players (in practice, soccer players) after anterior cruciate ligament injury. Fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers, while confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators.
paper.tldr: For female soccer players after an ACL injury, fear, uncertainty, low confidence and weak social support were reported as barriers to return, and confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity as helpers. The authors suggest considering these alongside physical milestones, but the evidence is perceptual and from a small number of studies.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, registered with the Open Science Framework on 14 April 2025. SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo and Embase were searched from inception on 1 May 2025 for original research on psychosocial factors and return to sport or physical activity in female players of any football code with a surgically or non-surgically managed ACL injury and a sample mean age of 18 or older. Two reviewers screened records, no quality appraisal was done, and findings were synthesized narratively into themes.
paper.findings: Seven studies (403 female players aged 16 to 56; 222 returned to sport and 181 did not) were included, five qualitative and two cross-sectional. Fear was reported in five studies and lack of confidence in three as barriers linked to returning at a lower level or not returning; uncertainty and poor social support were also perceived barriers. Confidence in healthcare professionals, motivation, positive social support and strong athletic identity were perceived facilitators, and one cross-sectional study found players who returned had higher motivation (p < 0.001).
paper.limitations: The review did not appraise study quality, did not distinguish sex from gender, and could not establish causal relationships because most included studies were qualitative. Outcome measures for return to sport and physical activity were inconsistent, and differences by surgical versus non-surgical management were not explored. The abstract reports 582 records screened and 74 full texts assessed, while the PRISMA diagram shows 581 and 73 plus one study from reference lists.
paper.practicalImplications: Return-to-sport planning for female soccer players after ACL injury can include attention to fear, confidence and social support alongside physical milestones. The authors suggest psychosocial screening and referral to a sport psychologist when needed, but the review does not test any screening tool or intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff working with female soccer players returning from ACL injury may find confidence, fear and team connection worth watching alongside physical testing, because players described these as shaping how they returned. The evidence is perceptual and does not set performance targets.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport planning in female soccer players after ACL injury: fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers, and confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity perceived facilitators. It cannot set return criteria, and it does not show whether addressing these factors changes return rates.
